segs.text: Module seven A, objective two. Relative against absolute bioavailability. F, the bioavailability factor, is the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation, with no units. Absolute bioavailability compares a dose given by an extravascular route, any route other than directly into the blood, here oral, with the same drug given intravenously, I V. An I V dose is placed entirely in the blood, so its F is one, and it is the standard. Relative bioavailability compares two formulations of the same drug, such as a tablet against an oral solution; neither is I V, so the reference product is the standard.

card.m: F: fraction of the dose reaching the circulation, no units
absolute: extravascular (here oral, po) against IV
IV: the whole dose in the blood → F = 1, the standard
relative: two formulations, neither IV; reference product = standard

segs.text: Both compare extent, so both compare areas under the curve, A U C. The I V dose is usually smaller than the oral dose, so each area is divided by its own dose, and F is the oral area per milligram over the I V area per milligram. So a larger oral area at the same doses gives a larger F. A larger oral dose that gives the same area gives a smaller F, because each milligram delivered less.

card.m: F = {{frac:AUC<sub>po</sub>/D<sub>po</sub>|AUC<sub>IV</sub>/D<sub>IV</sub>}}, area per mg against area per mg
AUC<sub>po</sub> higher, same doses → F higher
D<sub>po</sub> higher, same AUC<sub>po</sub> → F lower

segs.text: Written out, F abs equals A U C p o over A U C I V, times D I V over D p o, where p o means oral. The I V area is underneath because it is the comparator, and the I V dose is on top because the I V area was divided by it. Areas cancel with areas and milligrams with milligrams, so F has no units. She said, I want you to remember that the I V A U C is going to be in the denominator, right? That is what you are comparing it to.

card.m: IV area underneath, IV dose on top

segs.text: For relative bioavailability, F rel equals A U C A over A U C B, times D B over D A. A is the test product, and B the reference, whose area goes underneath; compared to the oral solution makes the solution B. An absolute F cannot be above one, because the I V reference already places the whole dose in the blood. A relative F can be above one, because the test product can do better than the reference. The textbook names a property or excipient of the test formulation, and her example was an old product, Bayer aspirin, that a newer one could exceed. And an F rel of one does not mean an absolute F of one, since the reference is not I V.

card.m: A = test; B = reference, in the denominator
her example: Bayer aspirin, an old product a newer one could exceed

segs.text: Her first practice problem asks the absolute bioavailability of a two hundred fifty milligram oral tablet. In six volunteers it gave an average A U C of one hundred one point five microgram hours per milliliter, and a one hundred milligram I V bolus gave seventy three point eight. The comparator is I V, so it is absolute, with the I V area underneath and the I V dose on top. The oral area is larger only because its dose is two and a half times as large; per milligram the tablet gives less. F abs is zero point five five, or fifty five percent: each milligram of the tablet delivers fifty five percent of what a milligram given I V delivers.

card.m: per mg: oral {{frac:101.5|250}} = 0.406; IV {{frac:73.8|100}} = 0.738 (mcg/mL)hr per mg

segs.text: Her second problem compares the same tablet with five milliliters of an oral solution holding two hundred fifty milligrams, average A U C ninety eight point seven six microgram hours per milliliter. It asks the bioavailability of the tablet compared to the oral solution, so it is relative, and the solution is B, underneath. The doses are equal, so only the area ratio is left, and F rel is one point zero three: the tablet delivers about three percent more than the solution. A solution has little or no formulation effect, so solution against I V shows the drug's own absorption, and tablet against solution isolates the formulation.

card.m: both oral, compared to the solution → F<sub>rel</sub>, solution = B
solution vs IV: the drug's absorption. tablet vs solution: the formulation

segs.text: The stem may only ask the oral bioavailability, or the bioavailability compared to another product. An I V comparator makes it absolute, and two products, neither of them I V, make it relative. Inverting the ratios is the usual wrong answer; for her first problem it gives one point eight two, and an absolute F above one shows the inversion. Asked in class which F can be greater than one, her answer was relative. The one point zero three shows similar extent, not bioequivalence, because no peak times were given, and the peak time is the rate in objective one. Absolute F is what turns an I V dose into an oral dose with the same area, in objective four, and she said she would focus more on absolute bioavailability.

card.m: the word absolute may be missing
IV comparator → F<sub>abs</sub>; two non-IV products → F<sub>rel</sub>
F<sub>rel</sub> = 1.03: extent similar, rate unknown → bioequivalence not shown
